newsitem.title: USA: Helms attacks Clinton plan to clear up UN arrears.
newsitem.headline: Helms attacks Clinton plan to clear up UN arrears.

text.p: The Clinton administration unveiled a plan on Wednesday to clear up about $1 billion in U.S. arrears to the United Nations but ran into criticism from Senate Foreign Relations Committee Chairman Jesse Helms.

Representative Bill Richardson, President Bill Clinton's nominee as U.N. ambassador, said the administration would seek funding to cover the arrears but would delay payment until the 1999 fiscal year, beginning on Oct. 1, 1998, and then pay only on condition that the United Nations met U.S. reform goals.

Congress has held up U.S. dues amid charges of U.N. waste and inefficiency. Helms told new Secretary-General Kofi Annan last week he would seek legislation setting "benchmarks" for reform that would have to be met before arrears were paid.

When Richardson said the administration was coming up with its own plan, Helms angrily charged that it was bypassing his committee with an "emergency supplemental appropriation" that would not necessarily go before the panel.

"I would consider it a breach of good faith and a blatant effort to circumvent this committee if this was done," the North Carolina Republican said. "This committee is not going to be shoved around as long as I'm chairman of it."
But Helms made clear his ire was aroused by the means, not by the ends. "I believe Mr. Annan genuinely wants to reform the United Nations and I genuinely want to help him," he said.

Richardson, a Democratic congressman from New Mexico who was testifying on his nomination for the U.N. post, did not say how much would be sought. but said it would be in the president's budget to be submitted to Congress on Feb. 6.

Republican Sen. Rod Grams of Minnesota said he had heard that the administration would request $912 million as a supplemental appropriation request and that he, like Helms, objected to this method of funding.
He told Richardson he would be disappointed it that were true because Secretary of State Madeleine Albright had given assurances the administration would work with Congress on the arrears issue.

Richardson said the United States owed the United Nations about $1 billion and the debt was likely to grow by $100 million a year. He said the administration wanted to work with Congress on a "reasonable approach" to pay off the debt and reduce U.S. financial obligations to the United Nations and other international organisations.

"With your support the United States would offer an advance appropriation, sufficient funding to cover our arrears, but it would not be made available until 1999 and would be disbursed only if our goals were met," he said.
Saying early congressional consideration of the package "would help us to leverage diplomatically the changes necessary to be negotiated this year," he asked the committee to keep an open mind.
Challenged by Helms, he said he was talking only about "concepts" that were "not set in stone," adding that the administration sought to work with the committee.

The administration effort to clear U.N. arrears faces resistance among many congressional Republicans who resent spending money on the world body. But Maryland Democrat Paul Sarbanes said the problem was undercutting the U.S. position at the United Nations. He defended the administration budget plan as necessary to "carve out a place" for arrears payment.

Richardson said the United States wanted to hold its peacekeeping contributions at 25 percent of the total U.N. budget for such operations and reduce regular contributions to 20 percent from 25 percent of the total U.N. budget.

He said the administration envisioned U.N. reforms that would maintain "at least zero growth" in its budget and streamline the secretariat and the "big three" affiliated agencies -- the World Health Organisation, the International Labour Organisation and the Food and Agriculture Organisation.
The reforms would also add Germany and Japan to the Security Council while preserving the prerogatives of the present five permanent members who have veto power.
Richardson received a friendly reception at the hearing, and his confirmation appeared assured.
